issues.legal_issue: The authority to prescribe a lower maximum rent for agricultural tenancies is constitutionally valid when it forms part of a law regulating landlord–tenant relations and providing relief to agricultural tenants.
material_facts: The law regulated relations between landlords and tenants of agricultural land and limited the rent a landlord could recover.
The law authorized the government to prescribe a lower maximum rent for land in particular areas or on another suitable basis.

A landlord challenged that authority under constitutional protections, and the law’s material rent provisions were substantially similar to provisions of an enactment previously considered by the Court.
The landlord argued that differences in the preamble, the treatment of irrigated and non-irrigated land, and the absence of a minimum rent made the authority invalid.
issues.conclusion: The statutory authority to prescribe a lower maximum rent was valid and constitutional; the asserted differences did not materially distinguish it from the substantially similar provision previously upheld.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied the reasoning in Vasantlal Maganbhai Sanjanwala v. State of Bombay, [1961] 1 S.C.R. 341, which upheld the corresponding rent-fixing provision in the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948. A law’s agrarian-reform purpose and tenant-relief scheme may be apparent from its provisions even if its preamble does not expressly state social justice as an object. A maximum rent ceiling need not distinguish between irrigated and non-irrigated land, and the absence of a minimum-rent provision does not invalidate the ceiling authority. The challenge invoked Articles 14, 19(1)(f), 26, 31 and 31A of the Constitution.

rule.if: agricultural_tenancy_law_challenge and law_regulates_landlord_tenant_relations and law_limits_agricultural_rent and rent_scheme_materially_similar_to_upheld_scheme

predicates.agricultural_tenancy_law_challenge: A landlord challenged the validity of a law governing rent in agricultural tenancies.
predicates.law_regulates_landlord_tenant_relations: The law regulates the relations between landlords and tenants of agricultural land.
predicates.law_limits_agricultural_rent: The law limits the rent recoverable for agricultural land and authorizes a lower maximum to be set.
predicates.rent_scheme_materially_similar_to_upheld: The law’s materially relevant rent-fixing scheme is substantially similar to one previously considered by the Court.

issues.definition: When a challenged agricultural-tenancy law regulates landlord–tenant relations, limits agricultural rent, and materially follows a rent-fixing scheme previously upheld, the authority to set a lower rent ceiling is valid.

issues.legal_issue: A government notification may set lower rent ceilings across all areas by using recognized land categories when the statutory baseline ceiling and the power to set lower ceilings are independent, coordinate rules.
material_facts: The law set a maximum rent for agricultural leases and authorized the government to set a lower maximum for lands in particular areas or on another suitable basis.
The government issued a notification setting different maximum rents for two recognized categories of land across the state: plains lands and hilly lands.
The categories reflected differences in rainfall, cultivation, living conditions, labour availability, and the quantity and quality of produce.
The landlord argued that the notification was invalid because the lower-ceiling power was an exception that could not displace the statutory ceiling throughout the state.
issues.conclusion: The notification was valid. The statutory baseline ceiling applied until a notification covered the relevant area; the power to set lower ceilings was an independent, coordinate provision, not an exception to the baseline rule, and the notification could cover all areas.
issues.legal_principle: The Court construed the two rent-fixing provisions as independent but coordinate: one established a baseline ceiling applicable to agricultural leases, while the other authorized lower ceilings by area or another suitable basis. The Court rejected the proposed application of the exception-swallowing-the-rule principle and distinguished Macbeth v. Ashley, (1874) L.R. 2 Sc. App. 352, where the challenged order was treated as an evasion of the statute rather than an honest exercise of the discretion conferred. The statute did not require any area to remain governed by the baseline ceiling after a notification was issued.

rule.if: rent_notification_challenge and law_sets_baseline_rent_ceiling and law_authorizes_lower_area_based_ceiling and notification_uses_recognized_land_categories and categories_reflect_relevant_land_differences

predicates.rent_notification_challenge: A party challenged a government notification that changed the maximum rent payable for agricultural land.
predicates.law_sets_baseline_rent_ceiling: The law establishes a baseline maximum rent for agricultural leases.
predicates.law_authorizes_lower_area_based_ceiling: The law authorizes the government to set a lower maximum rent for particular areas or on another suitable basis.
predicates.notification_uses_recognized_land_catego: The government set different maximum rents by dividing land into recognized categories, including categories applying across the state.
predicates.categories_reflect_relevant_land_differe: The categories correspond to differences in conditions relevant to cultivation and agricultural produce.

issues.definition: When a challenged rent notification uses recognized land categories reflecting relevant agricultural differences under a law that establishes a baseline ceiling and authorizes lower area-based ceilings, the notification is valid.
